title: Intro Chat: Senior Inference Candidate — Rowan Patel
topics: background, recent projects, inference runtime experience, quantization, kubernetes+on-prem, SLOs, culture fit
summary: 30–40 minute initial phone screen for Senior Inference Engineer. Candidate Rowan has strong background in model serving, worked on 8-bit quantization for transformer models, and led a small infra team. Discussed experience with batching, KV cache strategies, CUDA optimization, and on-prem VPC constraints. Agreed next steps: send take-home assignment and schedule technical deep-dive with infra team.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-11-04
Start: 09:30 PST
Duration: 40 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording)
Attendees: Ethan Brooks (Redwood), Priya Nair (Hiring Manager), Samir Gupta (SE), Olivia Tran (Recruiter), Rowan Patel (Candidate)

[00:00] Ethan: Hey Rowan, thanks for taking the time. Can you hear us ok?
[00:08] Rowan: Yeah loud and clear, thanks for having me.
[00:12] Priya: Great, we'll do a quick intros then move to your background and some technical questions. We're keeping this to 30–40.
[00:20] Rowan: Sounds good.
[00:22] Ethan: Quick housekeeping, this is a recorded screen, and then Priya will ask about your recent work. Olivia's here to take notes.
[00:30] Priya: Rowan, can you give a brief summary of what you've been working on at Updraft Labs the last two years?
[00:38] Rowan: Sure. So I was leading a three person infra team, focused on inference at scale for our conversational AI product. We built a serving layer on k8s with a custom autoscaler for GPU nodes, did a lot of model quantization work — mostly int8 and some 4-bit experiments — and implemented prefix caching to speed up repeated queries. I also owned the rollout process for new model versions and worked with product on latency SLOs.
[01:05] Samir: When you say prefix caching — is that in-memory KV cache per-node, or a distributed cache?
[01:12] Rowan: It's per-pod KV cache for the model KV state — a warm cache of recent prefixes keyed by request fingerprint. We experimented with a Redis-backed shared cache but found network hops killed tail latency. So we opted for per-node with a small sharding layer for sticky routing.
[01:29] Priya: That's similar to a lot of infra tradeoffs. Tell us about the quantization work — what toolchain and accuracy tradeoffs did you hit?
[01:38] Rowan: We used a mix — started with ONNX quantization pipelines and then moved to bitsandbytes style 8-bit kernels for transformer attention. We had to do per-layer calibration; attention layers were particularly sensitive so we left some layers in fp16. In production, 8-bit gave us about 2.5x throughput improvement and a small drop in rouge/acc metrics, but once we tuned the per-layer scaling and used outlier clipping the delta was acceptable.
[02:05] Ethan: Did you do any work on custom CUDA kernels or rely on vendor kernels?
[02:10] Rowan: Mostly vendor kernels and existing libraries, but I did prototype a fused attention kernel in CUDA for a 2k sequence use case; it cut per-step latency by ~20% on A100. It wasn't productized because of maintenance cost, but the proof-of-concept helped us optimize batching strategy.
[02:28] Samir: In terms of batching, do you use dynamic batching or fixed-size micro-batching? How do you handle latency-sensitive requests?
[02:36] Rowan: Dynamic batching — we implemented a multi-queue scheduler that prioritized low-latency routes. For high-priority requests we used a fast lane that bypassed big batches and used smaller batch sizes with dedicated pre-warmed pods. We tuned the scheduler using p95/p99 targets and simulated loads to find sweet spots.
[02:56] Priya: How do you measure cost vs latency tradeoffs? Any tooling or dashboards?
[03:02] Rowan: We had a cost telemetry pipeline — token-level accounting plus GPU utilization correlated to model versions. Dashboards showed cost per 1k tokens per model and we set cost budgets per feature. For decisions we ran A/B with quality metrics and cost impact.
[03:18] Olivia: quick clarifying q — have you worked with private deployments or VPC/on-prem setups?
[03:22] Rowan: Yes — we did an on-prem PoC for a healthcare client. Key constraints were no internet egress and HSM for keys. We packaged runtime as an air-gapped container and used an internal KMS adapter. The biggest challenge was debugging GPU driver mismatches across customer environment.
[03:41] Samir: Nice, that's relevant to our Private offering. Any experience with compliance — SOC2, audits?
[03:46] Rowan: I supported SOC2 readiness — created runbooks for data retention, access logs, and worked with security to collect audit evidence. I also helped set up RBAC mappings and SSO integration.
[03:55] Priya: Shifting gears — can you walk us through a production incident you owned?
[03:59] Rowan: Sure. One incident was a regression after a model rollout where tail latency spiked. Root cause was a combination of a change in prompt length distribution and a batching config that increased queued tokens; our autoscaler didn't spin up fast enough. I rolled back the model, adjusted batching thresholds, and added a canary with traffic shaping. Postmortem included changes to rollout policy and more rigorous pre-rollout load tests.
[04:25] Ethan: Nice, that's exactly the kind of ownership we like. Any experience mentoring engineers or hiring?
[04:30] Rowan: Yeah, I hired two infra engineers, did weekly 1:1s, and ran on-call rotations.
[04:35] Samir: Technical follow-up — what's your approach to thread safety and memory management for KV caches on GPUs? We sometimes see memory pressure when multiple models are loaded.
[04:44] Rowan: We separated model state from KV cache; KV cache lives in CPU memory with a fast path into GPU when needed. We used lock-free structures for read-mostly access and applied LRU segments to evict stale prefixes. For multi-model hosts we enforced soft memory quotas and would offload cold models to remote cold storage.
[05:07] Priya: Do you have any hands-on experience with compilation and kernel selection — like using Triton or custom compilers?
[05:13] Rowan: I used Triton a bit for kernel prototyping and relied on a compilation pipeline that chose between cuDNN, Triton, and vendor fused kernels based on sequence length heuristics. I haven't built a full compiler stack but I understand the tradeoffs.
[05:29] Ethan: Switching to culture — what are you looking for in a team and why Redwood?
[05:34] Rowan: I want an engineering-first org where infra work is product-facing — I like the idea of a company building inference primitives and shipping optimizations that impact customers. Redwood's unified serving approach and emphasis on observability resonates with me.
[05:47] Priya: Any questions for us about role, stack, or team?
[05:51] Rowan: A couple. First, how big is the infra team today and how autonomous is it?
[05:56] Samir: We have ~8 infra/platform engineers split across runtime, orchestration, and reliability. Teams are small and own from code to production.
[06:05] Rowan: Also curious about quantization strategy — do you prefer model-side quantization or runtime quantization?
[06:11] Priya: We try to provide model and runtime options; Redwood Optimize gives recommendations and runtime supports quantized kernels — it depends on workload.
[06:19] Rowan: Cool. Quick more technical — have you run cost regressions tied to batching changes? I ask because we had an incident where batching reduced latency but increased tokens due to repeated prefixes leading to higher token counts.
[06:30] Samir: Yep. We track token-level cost and have policies to detect regressions. We also run synthetic workloads to flag changes.
[06:39] Ethan: We're about halfway so we'll do one deep technical question and then wrap. Samir will pick.
[06:46] Samir: Imagine you have a 2k sequence model with spikes to 8k for some users. How would you architect routing and model selection to meet p95 latency SLOs while controlling cost?
[06:58] Rowan: I'd use model variants: short-context optimized model for typical 2k workloads and a second long-context variant for the outliers. Routing: detect sequence length at ingress and route short requests to the optimized model and long to the long-context model. For cost controls, put long-context requests through a throttled queue or a paid-tier fast lane. Also use prefix/KV caching for repeated context and cache warmers for scheduled users. For autoscaling, maintain a small pool of pre-warmed long-context nodes for fast cold-start.
[07:30] Samir: How about memory and KV cache when you have multi-tenant hosts?
[07:34] Rowan: enforce per-tenant quotas, use eviction policies tuned by recency and hit-rate estimators, and consider sharding hosts by tenant size. If tenants are noisy, move them to isolated pools.
[07:46] Priya: Good. Anything on observability you'd add?
[07:49] Rowan: Trace sampling tied to latency percentiles, token-level cost attribution, and synthetic canaries that exercise long-context paths.
[07:58] Ethan: Okay we're at ~35 minutes — last question: what would you need in a first 90 days?
[08:04] Rowan: I'd want a ramp plan: understand the existing runtime, run a couple of incident blameless postmortems, own a small project to improve a bottleneck (batching scheduler or cache), and mentor an engineer.
[08:16] Priya: That aligns. We'll follow-up with a technical deep-dive. Any final Qs from you?
[08:21] Rowan: Just one — what's the interview loop look like?
[08:24] Olivia: We'll do a 90-min deep technical with two engineers, a system design, and a culture/on-call panel. Then if it goes well, an exec conversation.
[08:33] Ethan: Great. We'll send next steps. Thanks for your time Rowan.
[08:36] Rowan: Thanks everyone. Appreciate it.

Notes on transcription: some technical terms may be transcribed slightly off (e.g., K-V cash, quantizashun), filler words removed in places for readability.
